summary:
Allwork.Space republishes a Fortune piece (by Muskaan Arshad, via Reuters Connect syndication) reporting that women now hold the majority of U.S. payroll jobs for only the third time in history, while still earning substantially less than men.

Key data: a National Association of Colleges and Employers study found class of 2023 bachelor's degree graduates started at an average of $59,778 for women versus $72,190 for men, roughly 83 cents on the dollar before careers begin. Previous female payroll majorities occurred briefly around 2010 during the Great Recession and in early 2020 before the pandemic, both driven by downturns wiping out male-dominated construction and manufacturing work. This crossover is different because it arrived without a recession.

Bureau of Labor Statistics figures cited show employed women grew by more than 870,000 over 12 months while men shed nearly 1.5 million jobs. In August, women accounted for 158,000 of 162,000 jobs added, with men just 2%. Roughly 7 million fewer men are employed than in the 1990s, and male labor force participation for those 20 and older fell to 69.4% in August 2026 from 75.8% in August 2006.

Explanations offered include video gaming as a cause of male retreat, and research by University of Connecticut economists Remy Levin and Daniela Vidart arguing that men entering weak labor markets become pessimistic and opt out. Laura Ullrich of the Indeed Hiring Lab calls the decline semi-permanent and structural.

On pay: women earn 81 cents per male dollar, a gap widening with age, totaling $542,800 less over a 40-year career and more than $1 million for women of color. Female-dominated fields (education, nursing, care work) pay less; women outnumber men 3 to 1 in teaching and 8 to 1 in nursing. Claudia Goldin's Nobel-winning research identifies parenthood as the biggest driver. The piece notes post-pandemic return-to-office mandates have disproportionately hit mothers who are primary caretakers.
